quote: “—for over thirty years,” Jeffreyssai said. “Not one of them saw it; not Einstein, not Schrödinger, not even von Neumann.”
content: The premise of the lesson is false for two of the three names. Von Neumann’s 1932 treatment applied the unitary laws to the apparatus and the observer and followed the chain as far as one liked; he saw that it never terminated in a single outcome and introduced the projection postulate to make it do so. Schrödinger, in his 1952 Dublin lectures, said that the equation taken seriously describes simultaneous alternatives all of which are real, and remarked that the idea would be regarded as lunacy (Bitbol, Schrödinger’s Philosophy of Quantum Mechanics, 1996). Everett’s thesis followed in 1957, thirty years after the 1927 Solvay conference, so “over thirty years” is the interval between the problem and the proposal the fiction treats as obvious. The Eld scientists did see it. What they did not do was conclude that seeing it settled anything, because the universal application of the laws left the Born statistics and the definiteness of experience unexplained, which is the point this book’s own quantum sequence concedes in its final essay. A parable that asks “how did they fail?” about a failure that did not occur teaches the lesson it was written to teach, and no other.

quote: The factor I had in mind, Brennan, was that Eld scientists thought it was acceptable to take thirty years to solve a problem.
content: The doctrine that major problems should yield in a month to sufficient speed of thought is not supported by what is known about creative problem-solving, and the sensei’s arithmetic (five minutes per insight, 5,760 insights a month) is not how insight works. Incubation, time away from a problem, reliably improves solution rates in the experimental literature (Sio & Ormerod (2009), a meta-analysis); expertise sufficient to see a hard problem’s structure takes on the order of a decade to acquire (Simon and Chase’s ten-year rule, 1973); and among eminent scientists, the quality of output is a roughly constant function of quantity across a career, so that the great results arrive at the rate of the ordinary ones (Simonton (1997)). Schrödinger’s month in Arosa, cited in the dialogue as “a famous historical success of our methodology,” came after twenty years of physics and six months of working through de Broglie, and the story of the mistress is Weyl’s gossip as reported by Moore’s biography, not a method. The author of the parable had, at the time of writing, been at his own central problem for over a decade without the month-long resolution the sensei demands, which is not a criticism of him but of the sensei.

quote: “Eld scientists were not trained…” Brennan paused. “No, untrained is not the concept. They were trained for the wrong task.
content: Brennan’s insight, that scientists are trained to work within an established body of knowledge and cannot practice the resolution of foundational confusion, is Kuhn’s account of normal science and paradigm shift (The Structure of Scientific Revolutions, 1962), presented here as a discovery made in four and a half minutes. Kuhn’s further point, which the parable omits, is that the training for normal science is what makes the anomalies visible in the first place, so that “trained for the wrong task” is also “trained for the only task that produces the problem.” The parable’s remedy, a Conspiracy that hoards open problems so that novices can practice on them, would remove the public accumulation of results that makes anomalies sharp enough to be recognized. Whether the resolution of confusion is a trainable skill separate from domain expertise is an empirical question; the transfer literature (annotated on Outside the Laboratory) gives no reason to think so, and the parable offers the assertion of a fictional teacher.
